We believe the AI debt boom is now driving Treasury yields higher.

Combined bond issuance from Big Tech firms, including their Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), is expected to surge to a record $320 billion this year.

This would mark a +$120 billion YoY increase, or +60%.

As a % of Treasury bond issuance, this is estimated to rise to a record ~70%.

This would be more than double the 30% recorded in 2025 and nearly 9x larger than 2024 levels.

In other words, Big Tech is now emerging as a serious competitor to the US government in the long-term debt market, increasingly competing for the same pool of buyers just as investors are demanding more compensation to hold this debt.

Big Tech debt is increasingly competing with US Treasuries for investor capital.

World Labs co-founders Justin Johnson and Dr. Fei-Fei Li say LLMs use next-token prediction, but spatial intelligence has its own equivalent:

Justin: "The soft definition of AI-completeness is there's this fundamental primitive that's an AI task. But if I could solve this AI task in its full, broadest generality, it would solve any intelligence problem."

"The classic example in LLMs is that next-token prediction is AI-complete... I think from Ilya: there's a mystery novel, the thing has to read the whole novel, and the final sentence is, 'And the killer was.' Predict the next token. You could basically frame any kind of intelligence task in terms of that."

"So clearly next-token prediction is something people believe is AI-complete."

"New-view prediction, this primitive that we have in Atlas, especially generative new-view prediction, is also AI-complete."

"I want to have a world where Martin is writing a proof of the Riemann hypothesis on the blackboard, and then the camera pans over to the next whiteboard."

Fei-Fei: "Evolution had to solve new-viewpoint prediction by making animals move. Nature gave animals eyes, but nature didn't give trees eyes. Why? Because when you move, you see a new viewpoint... We do believe very strongly that next-viewpoint prediction is the equivalent of next-token prediction."

@jcjohnss @drfeifei @martin_casado

Bitcoin and gold are increasingly moving together:

The 90-day correlation between Bitcoin and gold prices is up to +0.50, almost matching the all-time high set during the 2020 pandemic.

This figure has more than doubled since the start of the year.

By comparison, following the 2022 bear market recovery, the 90-day correlation rose to +0.30.

The recent surge accelerated following the US Treasury announcement on August 19th that it would at least double its buybacks of long-dated government debt, from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation.

Meanwhile, the 90-day correlation between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq 100 is down to ~0.30, a 1-year low.

Investors are increasingly turning to both gold and Bitcoin as hedges against currency debasement.

Hedge funds may now be a bigger risk to Treasuries than China:

For years, China was considered the biggest threat to the US Treasury market, as China’s official Treasury holdings grew to as large as $1.3 trillion in 2013, or 14% of the total.

This proportion, however, has steadily declined since then, to ~2%, its lowest since 2001.

Meanwhile, hedge funds now account for ~9% of all Treasuries outstanding, more than double their level seen in 2013.

Hedge funds now hold ~$2.6 trillion of Treasuries, with their gross exposure at ~$4.0 trillion, which includes short positions.

More importantly, these positions are increasingly debt-financed, with hedge fund repo cash borrowing surging to ~$3.0 trillion, more than doubling since early 2023.

This makes the Treasury market more vulnerable to forced selling, since a rise in yields can trigger margin calls for these leveraged funds, forcing them to sell Treasuries to raise cash and reduce their debt.

Hedge funds have become a major force in the Treasury market.

The 162,000 jobs everyone cheered came from waiters, bartenders, and a soccer tournament.

Food services and drinking places added 59,000 in August, the biggest gain by far and nearly 5x the 12-month average. Temporary FIFA World Cup hiring did most of the lifting. Information, finance, and government all shed jobs.

The highest-paying sectors are shrinking while low-wage temporary work carries the headline. Strip out the World Cup and this labor market is cooling.

Money market funds just hit a record $8 trillion. The mistake is assuming all of it is waiting to buy stocks.

Most of that pile stays parked at 4% and never moves. Watch the flow instead. Investors added a record $935 billion to cash in 2025 and are on track for about $500 billion more in 2026.

That marginal cash is the real dry powder. When the Fed cuts and 4% fades, even a slice of those inflows rotating into stocks and bonds is a powerful bid under every dip.

tweets.text:
The US now spends more servicing its debt than it spends on its entire military.

Federal interest payments hit $1.2 trillion a year, up from about $350 billion a decade ago. Every dollar of old debt rolls over at higher rates, so the bill feeds on itself.

To pay it, Treasury floods the market with new bonds, which pushes long yields higher, which raises next year's interest bill. This is the fiscal spiral, and it ends one of two ways. The Fed prints to cap yields, or the bond market forces the issue. Long bonds carry the cost either way.

🇺🇸 S&P is starting to measure how much room hyperscalers still have before their investment plans begin to threaten their ratings - FT
*AI boom is entering a phase where balance-sheet strength and the cost of capital will matter much more.

📊 S&P is not only looking at traditional bond debt as it uses a broader adjusted-debt framework that also captures part of leases, long-term power contracts, take-or-pay agreements, guarantees and other infrastructure-related obligations. Alphabet still has enormous headroom, Microsoft is also very strong despite the tighter constraints that come with a AAA rating, Meta still has a decent cushion while Amazon has much less room for error with leverage approaching the threshold associated with its current rating and debt headroom becoming very limited in some years.

⚠️ Oracle is clearly the most sensitive case as its adjusted debt-to-EBITDA could approach 4.5x which is roughly the level S&P associates with pressure on its BBB- rating. BBB- is the last rung of investment grade so a downgrade would push Oracle into high yield, potentially triggering forced selling from some investors, wider spreads and a higher cost of funding precisely when the company still needs to invest heavily in cloud and AI capacity. This could be one of the first real signs that the bond market is starting to impose discipline on the AI boom.

💰 As long as EBITDA keeps up, leverage remains manageable but the problem appears if AI monetisation is simply two or three years slower than expected. Revenues just need to arrive later while capex, leases, power contracts and infrastructure commitments are already locked in. That timing gap between immediate spending and future cash flow is where the real stress can emerge.

📈 The connection with long-term interest rates is fundamental too. S&P estimates that the six largest US hyperscalers could spend more than 7 trillion dollars over five years. Even if a large share is internally funded, that still represents a huge call on global capital at the same time as governments are financing massive deficits and utilities, power grids and data-centre operators are also raising enormous amounts of money.

➡ Hyperscalers remain extremely strong financially but they probably show the gradual end of a period in which AI financing looked almost unlimited.

*Ft link: https://t.co/fzNvzpvrz0

The world's reserve currency has lost about 9% of its value this year.

The dollar index is down roughly 9% from its January peak, near a 2-year low. Every dollar in your account now buys less of every hard asset on earth.

This is the flip side of a Fed cutting rates and printing while the debt compounds. It is why silver sits at decade highs and hard assets stay bid. A falling dollar is a slow tax on everyone who holds cash.

While yesterday’s ’s jobs report overstates the strength of the labor market, there is little doubt that underlying job growth has picked 
up.

Private-sector payroll growth averaged 75K in the three months to August. Outside of health care and education, the 3-month average climbed to 48K, after spending most of 2025 in negative territory. 

The payroll diffusion index rose to the highest level since 2024, signaling improved breadth of job gains. 

Temporary-help employment, a leading indicator for overall job growth, has begun to rebound. Both initial and continuing unemployment claims are running below last year’s levels.
